name: Engineering Leadership
description: Engineering organisation design, hiring, onboarding, performance and feedback, career ladders, coaching, delegation, culture, metrics and their misuse, predictability, on-call and incident culture, conflict and exits, inclusion, and planning with product for CTOs and engineering managers.

cards.subject: Stream-aligned team
says: delivers a continuous flow of change for a single business stream
owns its slice of the product end to end without handoffs
cards.use: want a team to ship user-facing change without waiting on others
not: exists only to maintain shared tooling for other teams

cards.subject: Platform team
says: offers internal services that other teams consume self-service
treats its platform as a product and other teams as its customers
cards.use: need to lift infrastructure burden off the product teams
not: approves every release made by product teams

cards.subject: Enabling team
says: coaches other teams in a capability they lack for a limited time
withdraws once the supported team is self-sufficient
cards.use: need several teams to adopt a practice such as test automation
not: takes over permanent operation of the capability it teaches

cards.subject: Complicated-subsystem team
says: owns a component that needs rare specialist knowledge
spares stream-aligned teams from learning a deep technical specialty
cards.use: have a part of the system that very few people can safely change
not: coaches teams for a few weeks and then disbands

cards.subject: Conway's law
says: observes that system design mirrors the communication structure of the organisation
explains why architecture boundaries tend to follow team boundaries
cards.use: wonder why three separate teams produced three separate services
not: says the codebase size determines how many teams are needed

cards.subject: Inverse Conway manoeuvre
says: shapes team structure on purpose to produce a wanted architecture
starts from the target design and then arranges the teams
cards.use: want a modular architecture while your teams are split by technical layer
not: mandates a new architecture while leaving the teams unchanged

cards.subject: Cognitive load
says: limits how much one team can own before quality and speed degrade
guides how many domains or services a team should take on
cards.use: see a team drowning in on-call, tooling and several unrelated domains
not: is reduced by adding more meetings to share context

cards.subject: Interaction mode
says: states whether two teams collaborate, facilitate or use a service from each other
makes the expected duration and intensity of cooperation explicit
cards.use: need to clarify whether two teams will pair closely or simply consume an API
not: is fixed once at company founding and never changes

cards.subject: Span of control
says: counts the direct reports a single manager has
leaves people without coaching when it grows too wide
cards.use: ask how many engineers one manager can realistically support
not: measures the number of services a team runs

cards.subject: Reorganisation
says: costs weeks of momentum while ownership and relationships reset
should be tied to a named problem rather than made out of habit
cards.use: are tempted to redraw the org chart after one missed deadline
not: improves delivery immediately because lines are clearer

cards.subject: Structured interview
says: asks every candidate the same questions in the same order
scores answers against a predefined rubric
cards.use: want comparable evidence across candidates
not: lets each interviewer improvise to follow instinct

cards.subject: Hiring scorecard
says: lists the competencies a role needs before any interview happens
keeps the panel judging the same criteria
cards.use: find interviewers disagreeing about what the role even requires
not: is written after the final candidate is chosen

cards.subject: Interview rubric
says: describes what weak, acceptable and strong answers look like per question
reduces differences between interviewers' standards
cards.use: see two interviewers rate the same answer very differently
not: lists the salary band for each level

cards.subject: Work-sample test
says: has the candidate do a small piece of realistic work
tends to predict job performance better than unstructured conversation
cards.use: need evidence of how a candidate actually builds or reviews code
not: is valid only when it takes several unpaid days

cards.subject: Live pairing interview
says: shows how a candidate collaborates and reasons out loud with an interviewer
exposes communication habits that a solo exercise hides
cards.use: want to see how a candidate handles hints and disagreement while coding
not: is best run with the candidate alone and unobserved

cards.subject: Independent scoring
says: has each interviewer record a rating before hearing the others
prevents anchoring on the most senior or loudest voice
cards.use: notice debriefs where the first speaker sways everyone
not: is done by averaging the scores after a group discussion

cards.subject: Debrief meeting
says: brings the panel together to weigh written evidence and reach a decision
is where disagreements between interviewers get resolved
cards.use: need to decide hire or no hire after all interviews are done
not: replaces written feedback with verbal impressions

cards.subject: Bar raiser
says: is an interviewer from outside the hiring team who guards the hiring standard
resists pressure to lower the bar when a role has been open a long time
cards.use: see a manager ready to accept a weak candidate because the role is urgent
not: is the hiring manager's closest friend on the team

cards.subject: Culture-fit screening
says: risks favouring candidates who resemble the current team
needs defining in terms of behaviours and values to be defensible
cards.use: hear an interviewer reject someone because 'I would not grab a beer with them'
not: is the most reliable predictor of job performance

cards.subject: Halo effect
says: lets one impressive trait colour judgment of every other competency
is countered by scoring each competency separately
cards.use: notice a candidate with a famous employer is rated well on everything
not: is a bias that only affects unqualified candidates

cards.subject: Cost of a bad hire
says: includes manager time, team morale and delayed delivery as well as salary
usually exceeds the cost of passing on a good candidate
cards.use: need to justify a slower and more rigorous hiring process
not: is limited to the recruiter's fee

cards.subject: 30-60-90 plan
says: sets expectations for a new hire's first three months in stages
moves from learning to contributing to owning
cards.use: are preparing the first quarter of a new engineer
not: fixes the hire's performance rating for the year

cards.subject: Onboarding buddy
says: pairs a new hire with a peer for day-to-day questions
lets the manager stay out of small how-do-I queries
cards.use: want a new hire to have a safe place to ask basic questions
not: is the new hire's line manager

cards.subject: First-commit goal
says: gets a new engineer's first change to production in the first days
proves that the build, review and deploy path works for them
cards.use: want a new hire to have shipped something by the end of week one
not: requires a large feature before the hire counts as onboarded

cards.subject: Pre-boarding
says: completes accounts, equipment and welcome contact before the start date
prevents a first day wasted on waiting for access
cards.use: see new hires spend day one without a laptop or logins
not: starts only on the morning of the first day

cards.subject: Time to first meaningful contribution
says: measures how quickly a new hire does work that the team values
points to slow environments or poor documentation when it is long
cards.use: want a single indicator of how well onboarding works
not: counts the hours a hire spends in training sessions

cards.subject: Onboarding retrospective
says: asks recent hires after a few weeks what slowed them down
feeds fixes straight back into the onboarding process
cards.use: want honest feedback while the new-hire view is still fresh
not: is held only with long-tenured engineers

cards.subject: SBI feedback
says: describes the situation, the behaviour and the impact
keeps feedback on observable facts rather than character
cards.use: need a simple structure for giving specific feedback
not: opens with the person's personality traits

cards.subject: Radical candor
says: combines caring personally with challenging directly
names the failure of being nice and saying nothing
cards.use: see a manager avoiding a hard message to protect feelings
not: says feedback should be blunt whether or not the relationship is good

cards.subject: Performance review cycle
says: summarises results and growth over a fixed period
should contain no surprises because feedback was given throughout
cards.use: find that a person is shocked by their half-year review
not: is the only moment feedback is given

cards.subject: Calibration session
says: compares ratings across managers to keep standards consistent
catches managers who rate too leniently or too harshly
cards.use: suspect one manager's 'meets expectations' means something different from another's
not: lets each manager decide ratings in complete isolation

cards.subject: Recency bias
says: overweights the last few weeks when judging a whole period
is reduced by keeping notes of achievements through the year
cards.use: see a review dominated by an incident from last month
not: gives extra credit to work finished long ago

cards.subject: Brag document
says: records an engineer's accomplishments and impact over time
gives a manager evidence for reviews and promotion cases
cards.use: want evidence ready when review season arrives
not: is written by the manager without input

cards.subject: Performance improvement plan
says: sets specific expectations and a time frame for recovery
should be used honestly rather than as paperwork before a dismissal
cards.use: have repeated, documented gaps after clear coaching
not: is a surprise announcement of dismissal

cards.subject: 360 review
says: collects feedback from managers, peers and reports
is best used for development rather than ratings alone
cards.use: want a manager to see how their direct reports perceive them
not: asks only the person's own manager

cards.subject: Objective and key results
says: pairs an ambitious objective with measurable key results
works poorly when tied directly to individual pay
cards.use: want a team to focus on a few outcomes in the quarter
not: lists every task a team will do

cards.subject: Impact over activity
says: judges engineers by the outcomes they enabled, not hours or lines written
guards against rewarding visible busyness
cards.use: hear that someone is a top performer because they always look busy
not: counts commits per week as the main signal

cards.subject: Career ladder
says: defines the expectations of each engineering level
gives people a shared view of what growth looks like
cards.use: are asked what an engineer must do to progress
not: fixes salaries for each level

cards.subject: Dual-track ladder
says: lets engineers advance as individual contributors or as managers
keeps senior technical people from being pushed into management
cards.use: worry about losing a great senior engineer who does not want to manage
not: makes management a higher level than any individual contributor role

cards.subject: Promotion packet
says: collects evidence that a person already works at the next level
is reviewed by people beyond the direct manager
cards.use: need to make a promotion case defensible and consistent
not: is based on time served at the current level

cards.subject: Sustained performance
says: requires evidence of operating at the next level over time
stops a single big project from triggering a promotion
cards.use: consider promoting someone after one good quarter
not: is satisfied by one standout project

cards.subject: Staff engineer
says: influences technical direction across several teams without managing them
is judged on scope and leverage, not only code output
cards.use: discuss what a senior individual contributor does beyond coding
not: is a manager with a larger team

cards.subject: Tech lead
says: guides the technical decisions of one team day to day
often combines delivery work with design leadership
cards.use: need someone to set technical direction for one team without managing people
not: handles the team's pay and performance reviews

cards.subject: Engineering manager
says: owns the people, team health and delivery of a group
hires, develops and removes obstacles for the team
cards.use: need someone accountable for team growth and outcomes
not: spends most of the week as the main committer

cards.subject: Sponsorship
says: has a senior person use their influence to advocate for someone's advancement
speaks for a person in rooms where they are absent
cards.use: see a capable engineer overlooked in promotion discussions
not: is the same as meeting for advice every month

cards.subject: Promotion before readiness
says: sets someone up to struggle in a role they are not yet performing
damages trust when peers see it as favouritism
cards.use: feel pressure to promote a flight-risk who is not yet operating at the next level
not: is the safest way to retain a strong performer

cards.subject: Level inflation
says: lowers the meaning of each level when promotions are given too easily
makes hiring and compensation harder to calibrate
cards.use: notice that most of the team has been promoted within two years
not: happens only when ladders are too strict

cards.subject: One-to-one
says: gives each report a regular private conversation with their manager
belongs to the report, who sets much of the agenda
cards.use: want a standing space to hear problems before they grow
not: is mainly a status report from the engineer

cards.subject: Skip-level meeting
says: has a manager meet the reports of their own reports
gives a view of team health without the middle manager's filter
cards.use: want to hear directly how a team feels about its manager
not: replaces the manager's own one-to-ones

cards.subject: Coaching conversation
says: asks questions that help the person find their own solution
resists handing over the answer too early
cards.use: want a report to build judgment rather than depend on you
not: tells the person exactly what to do

cards.subject: Mentor
says: shares experience and advice from a wider career
does not have to sit in the mentee's reporting line
cards.use: want someone outside the chain for career advice
not: decides the mentee's performance rating

cards.subject: GROW model
says: structures coaching as goal, reality, options and will
moves a conversation from description to commitment
cards.use: need a simple structure for a coaching conversation
not: is a way to score performance reviews

cards.subject: Growth plan
says: links a person's aspirations to specific projects and skills
is reviewed regularly in one-to-ones
cards.use: want to link someone's ambition to concrete development steps
not: is only written when someone is underperforming

cards.subject: Manager as a shield
says: absorbs pressure from above so the team can work
fails if it hides context the team needs for their decisions
cards.use: are tempted to hide a reorganisation rumour 'to protect the team'
not: is the best way to keep a team informed

cards.subject: Delegation
says: hands a task and its authority to another person
keeps accountability with the delegator
cards.use: are doing work that someone else could grow by owning
not: transfers all accountability along with the task

cards.subject: Situational leadership
says: adjusts how directive a manager is to the person's skill and confidence on the task
uses more direction for a novice and more autonomy for an expert
cards.use: need to manage a strong engineer new to a particular technology
not: applies one style to everyone for consistency

cards.subject: Micromanagement
says: checks every detail of how work is done
erodes trust and ownership in capable people
cards.use: find yourself rewriting your team's pull-request descriptions
not: builds a team's confidence over time

cards.subject: Manager of managers
says: leads through other managers instead of through the work itself
shifts the job to hiring, coaching and setting context for managers
cards.use: move from leading one team to leading several teams with their own managers
not: continues to review every technical decision directly

cards.subject: Decision-rights table
says: states who decides, who is consulted and who is informed
speeds up work by removing ambiguity about authority
cards.use: see a decision stall because nobody knows who can make it
not: requires consensus from every stakeholder

cards.subject: RACI
says: assigns responsible, accountable, consulted and informed roles
gives exactly one accountable owner for each outcome
cards.use: need to clarify roles on a cross-team initiative
not: names several accountable owners to share blame

cards.subject: Two-way door decision
says: can be reversed cheaply, so it should be decided quickly
is delegated to the people closest to the work
cards.use: see senior leaders slowed by approvals of easily undone choices
not: deserves the full committee review that one-way decisions get

cards.subject: Leader's intent
says: states the purpose and constraints of a task but not the method
lets people adapt when circumstances change
cards.use: want a team to improvise sensibly when plans break
not: lists the exact steps the team must follow

cards.subject: Management debt
says: builds up when a manager avoids hiring, feedback or clarity work
shows up later as slow delivery and attrition
cards.use: notice a manager who always chooses coding over people work
not: is solved by hiring a senior engineer

cards.subject: Psychological safety
says: is a shared belief that speaking up will not be punished or humiliated
lets people raise mistakes and doubts early
cards.use: see engineers hide errors until they become outages
not: means the team never disagrees or gives critical feedback

cards.subject: Blameless postmortem
says: examines how a system allowed a failure rather than who caused it
produces follow-up actions that change process or tooling
cards.use: need to learn from an outage without making someone the scapegoat
not: excuses people from accountability for their own work

cards.subject: Team charter
says: records a team's purpose, working agreements and ways of deciding
is written with the team rather than imposed on it
cards.use: want a new team to agree how it will work together
not: is a legal contract between departments

cards.subject: Working agreement
says: sets concrete rules for how the team collaborates, such as review times
is revisited when the team finds it no longer fits
cards.use: find reviews sitting for days with no shared expectation
not: is dictated by HR for the whole company

cards.subject: Engineering principles document
says: expresses a company's tie-breaker values for technical trade-offs
helps autonomous teams decide consistently without asking
cards.use: want teams to make similar trade-offs without central approval
not: lists the approved programming languages

cards.subject: Trust equation
says: builds trust from credibility, reliability and intimacy, reduced by self-interest
explains why dependable follow-through matters as much as expertise
cards.use: ask why a brilliant but unreliable lead struggles to earn trust
not: says trust grows mainly with technical skill

cards.subject: Fear of conflict
says: is a dysfunction where teams avoid honest debate to keep peace
produces artificial harmony and weak decisions
cards.use: see meetings end in polite agreement and then quiet resistance
not: is a sign of a healthy and aligned team

cards.subject: Hero culture
says: rewards individuals who rescue failing systems at the last minute
hides the fragile process that created the crisis
cards.use: notice the same engineer praised for weekend firefighting every month
not: encourages sustainable, preventive engineering

cards.subject: Leading by example
says: shapes culture through what leaders visibly do, not what they say
undermines stated values when behaviour contradicts them
cards.use: hear a leader praise work-life balance while sending midnight messages
not: is secondary to the values written on a poster

cards.subject: Rewarding the messenger
says: responds to bad news with thanks and a plan, not blame
encourages people to bring problems up early
cards.use: want teams to report slipping projects while there is time to act
not: publicly criticises the person who raised the problem

cards.subject: Deployment frequency
says: counts how often a team releases to production
rises as batches shrink and releases become routine
cards.use: want to see how often a team gets changes in front of users
not: measures how long an outage lasts

cards.subject: Lead time for changes
says: measures time from code commit to running in production
shows how long finished work waits in the pipeline
cards.use: want to see how quickly a committed change reaches users
not: measures time from idea to approved budget

cards.subject: Change failure rate
says: is the share of releases that cause a degradation needing a fix
is read alongside speed to check that quality has not dropped
cards.use: want to check that faster releases are not producing more incidents
not: counts every bug found before release

cards.subject: Time to restore service
says: measures how long it takes to recover from a production failure
rewards quick detection, rollback and clear runbooks
cards.use: want a delivery measure of resilience when things break
not: is the time to fix the root cause permanently

cards.subject: Cycle time
says: measures how long work takes from start to done
reveals queues and handoffs when it is much longer than active work time
cards.use: suspect tickets spend most of their life waiting
not: counts the hours engineers spend typing

cards.subject: Work in progress limit
says: caps how many items a team has open at once
shortens cycle time by forcing the team to finish before starting
cards.use: see everyone busy yet little work completed
not: raises throughput by starting more items in parallel

cards.subject: SPACE framework
says: views developer productivity across satisfaction, performance, activity, communication and efficiency
warns that no single metric describes productivity
cards.use: want a broader view than counting commits
not: reduces productivity to one velocity number

cards.subject: DORA metrics
says: group four measures of software delivery speed and stability
correlate with organisational performance in the research behind them
cards.use: need an evidence-based set of delivery measures
not: rank individual engineers for pay decisions

cards.subject: Goodhart's law
says: warns that a measure used as a target stops being a good measure
explains why teams game metrics tied to rewards
cards.use: watch a team split tickets to inflate a throughput number
not: says more measurement always improves behaviour

cards.subject: Developer experience survey
says: asks engineers how easily they can do their work
finds friction that delivery data alone does not show
cards.use: want to learn why builds and reviews feel slow
not: measures individual lines of code written

cards.subject: Flow efficiency
says: compares time work is actively worked on with total elapsed time
is low when items sit waiting between teams
cards.use: find work is active for two days in a six-week journey
not: measures how busy every engineer is

cards.subject: Story point
says: expresses relative effort and complexity rather than hours
is only meaningful within one team's own scale
cards.use: need a rough relative sizing for backlog items
not: converts directly into calendar days across teams

cards.subject: Velocity
says: reports how many story points a team completes per iteration
helps a team plan its own capacity and is not a productivity score
cards.use: want to forecast how much a team will finish next sprint
not: is a fair way to compare two teams

cards.subject: Throughput
says: counts how many work items are finished per time period
supports forecasting without estimating each item
cards.use: want to forecast without sizing every ticket
not: depends on story point totals

cards.subject: Monte Carlo forecast
says: simulates many outcomes from past throughput to give a range of dates
expresses delivery as a probability rather than a single date
cards.use: want to tell a stakeholder 'eighty-five percent likely by this date'
not: promises one exact delivery date

cards.subject: Cone of uncertainty
says: shows estimates narrowing as a project learns more
warns against fixed commitments at the very start
cards.use: are asked for an exact date before the problem is understood
not: says estimates are equally accurate at the beginning and end

cards.subject: Planning poker
says: has each team member privately propose an estimate and then compare
surfaces differing assumptions through discussion
cards.use: want the team to expose hidden assumptions while sizing
not: lets the loudest person set the final estimate

cards.subject: Small batch size
says: makes work easier to estimate and to finish
exposes problems earlier and lowers the cost of change
cards.use: see large tasks regularly slipping with surprises at the end
not: increases risk because every release is bigger

cards.subject: Estimate versus commitment
says: separates a forecast of likely effort from a promise to deliver
stops stakeholders turning a guess into a deadline
cards.use: hear a sales team quote an engineer's rough guess to a customer as a date
not: treats the two as the same thing

cards.subject: Dependency mapping
says: identifies work that waits on other teams
exposes cross-team risks before planning is committed
cards.use: find a project blocked by another team's unfinished component
not: is done once all coding has finished

cards.subject: On-call rotation
says: shares responsibility for responding to production alerts across engineers
needs fair scheduling and clear handover
cards.use: need someone available to respond to production problems out of hours
not: assigns the same engineer permanently to every incident

cards.subject: Follow-the-sun rotation
says: hands on-call duty between regions so that nobody works at night
depends on good handover notes between time zones
cards.use: have engineers in several time zones and want to avoid night pages
not: has one region cover every night shift

cards.subject: Escalation policy
says: defines who is alerted next if a page goes unanswered
stops a single missed alert from becoming a long outage
cards.use: need to guarantee that a missed page reaches somebody else
not: decides who is blamed for the incident

cards.subject: Incident commander
says: coordinates the response without necessarily fixing the problem
keeps one person responsible for decisions and communication
cards.use: see an outage where six engineers talk at once and nobody leads
not: is the engineer who wrote the failing code

cards.subject: Severity level
says: classifies an incident by its impact on users and the business
sets the urgency and who must be woken
cards.use: need to decide whether a problem justifies waking people at night
not: is a rating of the responder's performance

cards.subject: Alert fatigue
says: desensitises responders when pages are frequent or not actionable
is reduced by removing noisy alerts and tuning thresholds
cards.use: hear on-call engineers ignore pages because most are false alarms
not: improves response because alerts feel routine

cards.subject: Toil
says: is repetitive manual work that grows with the service and adds no lasting value
should be capped so on-call time includes improvement work
cards.use: see on-call engineers spend their week restarting the same service by hand
not: is the creative design work done by senior engineers

cards.subject: Error budget
says: is the amount of unreliability a service may spend before releases slow
turns the balance between speed and stability into an agreed number
cards.use: want an objective rule for when to pause features and fix reliability
not: is a financial budget for incident costs

cards.subject: Service level objective
says: sets a target for reliability measured against a defined indicator
is chosen below one hundred percent on purpose
cards.use: need a shared target for how reliable a service must be
not: promises compensation to customers when missed

cards.subject: Runbook
says: gives step-by-step instructions for handling a known alert
reduces the knowledge needed to respond at 3am
cards.use: want a new on-call engineer to handle a known alert safely
not: replaces the need for any monitoring

cards.subject: Five whys
says: asks why repeatedly to move from a symptom toward a systemic cause
can wrongly stop at a single human error if used carelessly
cards.use: find a postmortem concluding 'an engineer made a typo'
not: is a requirement to find exactly five causes

cards.subject: Underperformance diagnosis
says: separates lack of skill, lack of will and lack of clarity before choosing a response
decides whether the fix is training, motivation or expectations
cards.use: must decide what to do about an engineer who keeps missing targets
not: assumes poor motivation as the default cause

cards.subject: Expectation-setting conversation
says: puts what is expected in writing and agrees it before performance is judged
makes later feedback fair and specific
cards.use: hear someone say they never knew what was expected of them
not: relies on the job title alone

cards.subject: Documented feedback
says: records conversations and agreed actions in writing
protects both the employee and the company if the case escalates
cards.use: are having a second conversation about the same problem
not: replaces speaking to the person directly

cards.subject: Dismissal conversation
says: is short, clear and respectful, with the decision already made
leaves out debate or fresh warnings
cards.use: are about to tell an employee their employment is ending
not: opens a long negotiation about whether the decision should stand

cards.subject: Layoff communication
says: explains the business reason plainly and treats affected people with dignity
must reach the remaining team promptly to rebuild trust
cards.use: have to announce redundancies to the whole engineering organisation
not: lets rumours spread so people can prepare

cards.subject: Exit interview
says: asks a departing employee why they leave and what could improve
gives data on patterns only if answers are collected and acted on
cards.use: want to learn why valuable engineers keep resigning
not: is the same as a performance review

cards.subject: Stay interview
says: asks current high performers what keeps them and what would make them leave
finds retention risks before a resignation arrives
cards.use: want to learn what would make a valued engineer stay
not: is held only after someone resigns

cards.subject: Counter-offer
says: tries to retain a resigning employee with extra pay or title
often fails to fix the underlying reason they wanted to leave
cards.use: have a strong engineer who resigned for a better offer
not: usually solves the reason for resignation

cards.subject: Conflict mediation
says: brings both parties to talk through the issue with a neutral facilitator
aims at a working agreement, not at deciding who is right
cards.use: have two engineers who stopped speaking after an argument over design
not: picks a winner after hearing the louder side

cards.subject: Disagree and commit
says: asks people to support a decision wholeheartedly after voicing disagreement
works only after everyone has had a real chance to be heard
cards.use: need the team to move forward after a heated technical debate
not: requires every person to be convinced first

cards.subject: Brilliant jerk
says: delivers strong individual output while damaging the people around them
costs the team more than the output is worth when left unaddressed
cards.use: have a top coder who regularly belittles reviewers
not: should be protected because of their output

cards.subject: Tolerated low performance
says: shifts extra load onto peers who stay productive
damages team morale the longer it continues
cards.use: see the team quietly covering for one colleague for months
not: is kind to the rest of the team when it is postponed

cards.subject: Headcount plan
says: links hiring numbers to the work the business needs delivered
accounts for attrition and the time new hires need to become productive
cards.use: must propose how many engineers to hire for next year
not: adds engineers whenever a deadline is missed

cards.subject: Capacity planning
says: estimates the work a team can absorb after leave, on-call and meetings
stops the roadmap from assuming full availability
cards.use: find the roadmap assumes every engineer is free all week
not: counts every working day as productive time

cards.subject: Brooks's law
says: observes that adding people to a late project makes it later
stems from onboarding and communication overhead
cards.use: are asked to add ten engineers to a project three weeks before its date
not: says more people always shorten the schedule

cards.subject: Build, buy or partner
says: compares own development, purchase and partnership as sourcing choices
weighs differentiation against total cost of ownership
cards.use: need to decide whether to write a payments feature or license one
not: always favours writing everything in-house

cards.subject: Total cost of ownership
says: includes maintenance, operations and staffing as well as purchase price
prevents choosing an option that is cheap only on day one
cards.use: compare a free open-source tool with a paid service
not: is the licence price alone

cards.subject: Engineering budget
says: covers people, tools, cloud and training for the year
is easier to defend when tied to outcomes the business values
cards.use: must defend an annual budget to the finance team
not: is only the cost of salaries

cards.subject: Technical debt backlog
says: tracks known shortcuts together with their cost to the business
lets managers weigh repayment against features openly
cards.use: keep arguing about refactoring without any shared list
not: is hidden from product managers to avoid friction

cards.subject: Technical debt allowance
says: reserves a steady share of capacity for repaying debt
avoids negotiating every cleanup against every feature
cards.use: want debt repayment to survive deadline pressure
not: is spent only after all features ship

cards.subject: Debt interest
says: is the extra effort every future change costs because of an old shortcut
guides which debt to repay first
cards.use: need to decide which of several shortcuts to fix first
not: is zero until the system fails

cards.subject: Product trio
says: brings product, design and engineering leads together to shape work
finds feasibility and design problems before delivery starts
cards.use: find designs reaching engineers with no technical input
not: has engineering receive finished specifications and build them

cards.subject: Dual-track discovery
says: runs learning about problems alongside building the delivery work
keeps the backlog fed with validated ideas
cards.use: see teams run out of well-understood work or build unvalidated features
not: finishes all discovery before any build starts

cards.subject: Engineering pushback
says: explains cost, risk and alternatives to product rather than a flat no
offers options so decisions rest on trade-offs
cards.use: are asked to commit to an unrealistic deadline from product
not: refuses all requests that exceed capacity without explanation

cards.subject: Roadmap
says: communicates planned direction and priorities over time
is a statement of intent and not a delivery contract
cards.use: are asked for a plan stakeholders can follow for the next two quarters
not: is a fixed commitment to exact dates

cards.subject: Asynchronous communication
says: lets people respond on their own schedule instead of live
relies on written context that stands alone
cards.use: need to work across several time zones without constant meetings
not: requires everyone to be online simultaneously

cards.subject: Written decision record
says: captures a decision and its reasoning for later readers
spares remote teams from repeating the same debate
cards.use: keep re-debating a choice that was settled months ago
not: is written only for the decider

cards.subject: Core-hours window
says: sets a period when everyone is available for live collaboration
balances flexibility with the need for shared time
cards.use: have hybrid staff in several cities who need some overlap
not: requires every person to work identical hours

cards.subject: Proximity bias
says: favours people seen in the office when promotions and projects are handed out
is countered by judging on outcomes and by deliberate fairness
cards.use: notice remote engineers are passed over for interesting work
not: helps remote employees get recognition

cards.subject: Remote-first
says: designs every process as if all staff were remote
stops office attendees from getting hidden advantages
cards.use: want remote and office staff to have the same access to decisions
not: treats the office as the real place decisions happen

cards.subject: Inclusive job description
says: removes unnecessary requirements and exclusionary wording
widens the pool of qualified applicants
cards.use: find that few women or career changers apply to your roles
not: lists every possible skill to deter weak applicants

cards.subject: Diverse slate
says: requires a qualified shortlist that includes under-represented candidates before deciding
widens the candidate pool without lowering the standard
cards.use: see shortlists drawn almost entirely from one network
not: fills a quota with candidates who do not meet the bar

cards.subject: Blind screening
says: hides names and similar details when first reviewing applications
reduces the chance that first impressions rest on irrelevant traits
cards.use: want to limit unconscious bias at the résumé stage
not: removes the need for structured interviews

cards.subject: Pay equity review
says: compares compensation for similar roles across groups to find unexplained gaps
corrects differences that cannot be justified by role or level
cards.use: discover that two engineers at the same level have an unexplained pay gap
not: is needed only when an employee complains

cards.subject: Inclusive meeting
says: gives quieter people an agenda and a chance to speak
stops a few voices from dominating a discussion
cards.use: notice that the same three people speak in every design review
not: rewards the person who talks the most

qa.q: A team of eight builds, deploys and operates a checkout flow and keeps waiting on a separate infrastructure group for environments. What change best reduces the waiting?
qa.right: Provide self-service environments through an internal platform team
wrong: Move the infrastructure group's approval step earlier in the process
Add a weekly meeting where both groups review the environment queue
Hire two more people into the infrastructure group's approval queue
qa.why: A platform team removes the handoff by turning infrastructure into a self-service product; faster approvals keep the dependency.

qa.q: A new service was split across three teams and now every feature needs all three to coordinate. Which idea most directly explains this?
qa.right: System structure tends to copy the communication structure of the teams
wrong: Larger teams always produce larger codebases
Microservices must always have one team each
Coordination cost falls as the number of services grows
qa.why: Conway's law: architecture mirrors team communication paths.

qa.q: You manage 14 engineers directly and one-to-ones keep being cancelled. Which action is the best first move?
qa.right: Appoint team leads or managers to bring direct reports to a workable number
wrong: Shorten every one-to-one to ten minutes
Move all one-to-ones to a group meeting
Ask engineers to send written updates instead of meeting
qa.why: A span that wide cannot be coached well; restructuring reporting lines restores real one-to-ones.

qa.q: A candidate from a famous employer interviews well, but no interviewer probed testing. How should the panel handle testing in the debrief?
qa.right: Score each competency on its own evidence and mark testing as not assessed
wrong: Give testing the same score as the other areas
Treat testing as a strength because of the employer
Ask the candidate's former employer for a general opinion instead
qa.why: Scoring each competency separately counters the halo effect; unassessed areas should not be filled in by assumption.

qa.q: Three interviewers disagree about a candidate. The most senior spoke first in the debrief and the rest then agreed with him. What process change fixes this?
qa.right: Have everyone submit written ratings before the discussion starts
wrong: Let the most senior person speak last but keep the same format
Add one more interviewer to each panel
Ask the recruiter to chair the debrief
qa.why: Independent scoring prevents anchoring on whoever speaks first.

qa.q: A hiring manager wants to drop the coding exercise for an urgent role because the person seems smart. What is the strongest response?
qa.right: Keep the same assessment so candidates are compared on the same evidence
wrong: Waive it for this candidate only because the role is urgent
Replace it with a longer informal chat about their last job
Let the candidate pick whichever stage they prefer
qa.why: Consistent evidence matters most under pressure; shortcuts raise the risk of a costly bad hire.

qa.q: A new engineer joined three weeks ago and still has not shipped anything. Which cause should you check first?
qa.right: Whether the setup, access and review path actually let them make a change
wrong: Whether the engineer lacks motivation
Whether the engineer should move to a different team
Whether their salary was set too low
qa.why: Slow first contribution usually points to onboarding friction before personal causes.

qa.q: Every new starter asks you the same five questions about local setup. What is the best long-term fix?
qa.right: Write the answers into maintained documentation and improve it with each new hire
wrong: Answer faster by pinning a message in chat
Ask each new hire to figure it out alone to learn
Assign a senior engineer to answer for the next year
qa.why: Documentation fixes the cause once; answering individually repeats the cost.

qa.q: An engineer who heard nothing negative all year receives a low rating at review. What is the main failure?
qa.right: Feedback was not given in time for the person to act on it
wrong: The rating scale was too coarse
The engineer was not on a performance plan
The review should have been done by a peer
qa.why: Reviews should hold no surprises; feedback has to be continuous.

qa.q: You must tell an engineer that her pull requests often arrive without tests. Which wording follows the situation-behaviour-impact model?
qa.right: In yesterday's billing PR there were no tests, so the reviewer had to check behaviour by hand and the release slipped a day
wrong: You are careless about testing and should try harder
Everyone says your work has quality problems
I'd like you to be a better engineer in general
qa.why: SBI names a specific situation, the observable behaviour and its impact.

qa.q: Two managers rate nearly everyone 'exceeds expectations', while a third rarely does. What should the calibration session do?
qa.right: Compare evidence across the three and align what each rating means
wrong: Average the three managers' ratings into a single distribution
Ask the strictest manager to rate everyone
Cancel ratings for the year
qa.why: Calibration exists to align standards by comparing evidence, not by averaging.

qa.q: Your review draft is dominated by an incident from last month although the engineer delivered well all year. What bias is at work and what helps?
qa.right: Recency bias; keep notes of achievements through the year
wrong: Halo effect; add more peer reviewers
Proximity bias; hold reviews in person
Confirmation bias; remove the manager's input
qa.why: Reviewers overweight recent events; ongoing notes counter it.

qa.q: An engineer has missed deadlines for three months. She has the skills but says she is unsure what the priorities are. What is the best next step?
qa.right: Clarify the priorities and expectations in writing and check progress soon
wrong: Place her on a formal performance plan immediately
Reassign her work without telling her
Wait until the next review cycle
qa.why: Diagnosing the cause first shows it is a clarity problem, not skill or will.

qa.q: An engineer delivers one outstanding project and asks for promotion, but his level behaviours elsewhere are inconsistent. What is the best answer?
qa.right: Explain the gap and agree what evidence over time would support the case
wrong: Promote now to keep him from leaving
Decline without explanation
Promote him but with a probation period
qa.why: Promotion rests on sustained performance at the next level, with transparent criteria.

qa.q: A senior engineer says she has no wish to manage people but wants to keep growing. Which structure helps most?
qa.right: A parallel individual-contributor track with senior levels of equal standing
wrong: Making her team lead and keeping her title the same
A one-off bonus instead of a new level
Moving her into management for the pay
qa.why: A dual-track ladder lets technical staff progress without becoming managers.

qa.q: A capable engineer is repeatedly passed over in promotion talks because senior leaders do not know her work. What would a sponsor do?
qa.right: Advocate for her work in rooms where she is not present
wrong: Give her feedback on her presentation style
Suggest she network more
Meet her monthly for career advice
qa.why: Sponsorship is active advocacy; mentoring gives advice.

qa.q: In a one-to-one, a report asks you which of two designs to choose. You want him to build judgment. What is the best response?
qa.right: Ask what trade-offs he sees and which option he would pick and why
wrong: Tell him the answer to save time
Say it is his job to decide and leave
Suggest asking the tech lead
qa.why: Coaching questions build judgment rather than dependency.

qa.q: A middle manager's team reports through her, and you hear problems only after they have grown. Which step gives the most direct view?
qa.right: Hold skip-level meetings with her team while keeping her informed
wrong: Join her team's stand-ups daily
Send an anonymous survey every week
Ask her to report more often
qa.why: Skip-levels give an unfiltered view while respecting the manager's role.

qa.q: You just became a manager of managers and still review every pull request personally. What is the most likely consequence?
qa.right: You become a bottleneck and your managers do not grow
wrong: The teams ship faster
Your span of control shrinks
Technical quality becomes less consistent
qa.why: The job moves to setting context and developing managers; staying in the detail blocks delegation.

qa.q: You delegated a migration to an engineer and she is making slower progress than you expected. You are accountable for the result. What is best?
qa.right: Check in on agreed milestones, ask what is blocking her and offer help without taking over
wrong: Take the task back and finish it yourself
Check every commit each day
Tell her you are no longer responsible
qa.why: Delegation keeps accountability with the manager; support should match the person's need.

qa.q: A decision about renaming an internal API field is waiting on four approvals across teams. What principle applies?
qa.right: Decide quickly with those closest, because the choice is easy to reverse
wrong: Require consensus from all teams for traceability
Escalate to the CTO so the decision is final
Postpone until a full design review is possible
qa.why: Two-way door decisions should be made fast by those closest to the work.

qa.q: After an outage, the report says a developer pushed a bad config. What is the best postmortem response?
qa.right: Ask how the system allowed a bad config to reach production and what will prevent a repeat
wrong: Record the developer's name so the pattern is visible
Close the report as human error
Add a rule telling developers to be more careful
qa.why: Blameless postmortems look for system causes and fix the process.

qa.q: Engineers stay silent in design reviews and mistakes appear only in production. What is the likely underlying issue?
qa.right: Low psychological safety
wrong: Too many senior engineers
Reviews held too early
Weak documentation tools
qa.why: Silence and hidden errors are signs that speaking up feels unsafe.

qa.q: A manager praises work-life balance in town halls but sends messages at midnight and expects replies. What will the team most likely follow?
qa.right: The behaviour they see
wrong: The statement made in town halls
The written values
The HR policy
qa.why: Culture follows what leaders visibly do.

qa.q: A team's dashboard shows 90 commits a week per engineer and leaders celebrate it. Which concern is most valid?
qa.right: Commit counts are a vanity metric that can be gamed and tell little about outcomes
wrong: Commits are too hard to count
The team needs more engineers to raise the number
Commits should be measured per day
qa.why: Activity counts are easily inflated; outcome measures matter more.

qa.q: Your CEO wants to rank engineers by story points completed. What is the best reply?
qa.right: Points are relative to each team, so they cannot fairly compare people
wrong: Points are accurate enough if everyone estimates carefully
Rank by commits instead
Rank by hours logged
qa.why: Story points are a team-level planning tool; comparing individuals invites gaming.

qa.q: A team doubles its deployment frequency but its change failure rate also rises sharply. What is the right reading?
qa.right: Speed has outrun quality and practices such as testing and rollout need attention
wrong: The team is performing better overall
The failure rate figure is irrelevant
Deployment frequency should be cut back without further review
qa.why: DORA measures are read together; speed and stability should both improve.

qa.q: A ticket takes 30 days from start to done but only 3 days of hands-on work. Which measure and fix fit best?
qa.right: Flow efficiency is low; look for queues and handoffs
wrong: Velocity is low; add more engineers
Change failure rate is high; add tests
Deployment frequency is high; reduce releases
qa.why: Most of the elapsed time is waiting, so find queues, not effort.

qa.q: Management starts rewarding teams for lowering the number of reported bugs, and soon bug reports drop while customer complaints rise. Which law explains this?
qa.right: Goodhart's law
wrong: Brooks's law
Conway's law
Parkinson's law
qa.why: A measure that becomes a target stops measuring reliably.

qa.q: A stakeholder asks for an exact date for a project that has only been outlined. What is the best way to respond?
qa.right: Give a probabilistic range and refine it as the team learns
wrong: Give a single date with padding
Refuse to estimate
Quote the earliest possible date
qa.why: Early estimates carry wide uncertainty; ranges convey that honestly.

qa.q: A project is already late and your director proposes adding eight engineers. What is the likely effect?
qa.right: The project gets later for a while because of onboarding and communication overhead
wrong: The project finishes sooner immediately
Quality improves with more reviewers
The schedule is unaffected
qa.why: Brooks's law: adding people to a late project slows it.

qa.q: A sales lead tells a customer 'engineering said about June' after a quick conversation. What practice would have prevented this?
qa.right: Separating a rough estimate from a commitment and sharing it only as a forecast
wrong: Banning conversations with sales
Providing exact estimates to sales instantly
Adding buffer to every estimate secretly
qa.why: Forecasts and commitments are different, and the difference has to be explicit.

qa.q: A team sizes every task in hours but regularly finishes at about twice the estimate. Which approach gives the best forecast?
qa.right: Use historical throughput to forecast, rather than adjusting each estimate
wrong: Double every estimate
Estimate in smaller units of minutes
Ask engineers to work faster
qa.why: Historical data forecasts more reliably than adjusting individual guesses.

qa.q: An on-call engineer is paged about 15 times each night and most pages need no action. What is the first priority?
qa.right: Remove or tune non-actionable alerts
wrong: Rotate more engineers into the schedule
Pay a bonus for night work
Tell the team to respond faster
qa.why: Alert fatigue is solved by making alerts actionable.

qa.q: During a major outage six engineers are talking at once and executives keep asking for updates in the same channel. What roles are missing?
qa.right: An incident commander with a communications lead
wrong: A developer manager to assign blame
An extra engineer to write the fix
A product owner to prioritise features
qa.why: Clear coordination and separate communications let responders focus.

qa.q: The service has exhausted its error budget for the quarter. What should the policy say?
qa.right: Slow feature releases and invest in reliability until the budget recovers
wrong: Ignore the budget until customers complain
Raise the reliability target to 100 percent
Add more on-call engineers only
qa.why: Error budgets give an objective rule to rebalance speed and stability.

qa.q: A critical engineer is always praised for rescuing releases at the last minute. What should a thoughtful manager worry about?
qa.right: The fragile process that keeps producing the crisis
wrong: That other engineers will get jealous
That the engineer will ask for a raise
That the rescues cost too much overtime pay
qa.why: Hero culture hides systemic problems and creates single points of failure.

qa.q: Two senior engineers have stopped communicating after a design dispute, and the team is picking sides. What should you do first?
qa.right: Meet each privately and then facilitate a conversation between them focused on a working agreement
wrong: Let them sort it out
Pick the technically better design and tell them to comply
Move one of them to another team
qa.why: Early facilitation aims at a workable agreement before the split deepens.

qa.q: The team debated a decision for weeks and it was finally taken, but one engineer still disagrees. What do you ask of her?
qa.right: Voice her view fully, then support the decision wholeheartedly
wrong: Keep objecting until she is convinced
Stay silent and avoid the work
Wait for the decision to be reversed
qa.why: Disagree and commit works after a genuine hearing.

qa.q: A top-performing engineer regularly belittles colleagues in code review, and two juniors are considering leaving. What is the right action?
qa.right: Address the behaviour directly with clear expectations and consequences
wrong: Ignore it because the output is valuable
Move the juniors to other teams
Raise the engineer's pay to keep him
qa.why: Output does not justify behaviour that damages the team; delay costs more people.

qa.q: A strong engineer hands in her notice and your director suggests a counter-offer with extra pay. What is the biggest risk?
qa.right: The reasons she wanted to leave remain, so she may leave later anyway
wrong: She will refuse the offer
It will cause legal problems
Other employees will not hear about it
qa.why: Counter-offers rarely address the underlying reason for leaving.

qa.q: A colleague on the team has underperformed for months and others quietly cover for her. What is the cost of waiting?
qa.right: Peers carry extra load and lose trust in the manager
wrong: Nothing, as the work still gets done
The colleague will improve with time alone
The company saves salary costs
qa.why: Delay harms the rest of the team more than most managers expect.

qa.q: You are told to cut a tenth of the engineers. How should you speak to the remaining team?
qa.right: Explain the reason plainly and quickly and set out what happens next
wrong: Wait until the rumour settles
Say the cuts are over without being sure
Let managers decide what to say individually
qa.why: Prompt, honest communication rebuilds trust after layoffs.

qa.q: Finance asks why the engineering budget is rising while delivery has not. What helps most when defending it?
qa.right: Linking spend to outcomes the business values and being open about trade-offs
wrong: Showing the headcount list
Pointing out that peers spend more
Promising to cut it next year
qa.why: Budgets are defended with outcomes, not totals.

qa.q: Product wants to ship a feature that ignores a known weakness in the billing code. You believe the risk is real. What is the best approach?
qa.right: Present the cost and risk with options and let the decision rest on trade-offs
wrong: Refuse to start until the weakness is fixed
Agree silently and note it privately
Ask the CEO to overrule product
qa.why: Pushback works when it offers choices and consequences, not a flat no.

qa.q: Teams argue every sprint about whether to spend time on refactoring. Which arrangement fixes the argument?
qa.right: Reserve a fixed share of capacity for debt and track the cost of key items
wrong: Allow refactoring only after releases
Let each engineer decide alone
Stop all refactoring for the year
qa.why: A standing allowance removes repeated negotiation.

qa.q: Designs arrive after a three-month design phase and engineers say they cannot build them in time. What practice would help?
qa.right: Involve engineering in discovery alongside product and design
wrong: Add a design review before release
Let engineers redesign the screens
Skip the design phase
qa.why: A product trio finds feasibility problems before delivery starts.

qa.q: Remote engineers rarely get high-visibility projects although their results are strong. What is the most likely problem?
qa.right: Proximity bias in how work is assigned
wrong: A weaker internet connection
Lower performance in remote roles
Lack of mentoring programmes
qa.why: Teams favour people they see; deliberate processes counter it.

qa.q: Your hiring shortlist is drawn almost entirely from employees' personal networks. What is the strongest step?
qa.right: Require a qualified, diverse slate and widen sourcing before deciding
wrong: Lower the bar for under-represented candidates
Stop employee referrals
Drop the job description
qa.why: Widening sourcing keeps the bar and widens the pool.

qa.q: Which description is the best fit for a staff engineer?
qa.right: Sets technical direction across teams through influence rather than line management
wrong: Manages a team of engineers
Handles the build pipeline
Is a senior developer with a new title
qa.why: The role is judged on scope and leverage, not people management.

qa.q: What is the main purpose of a working agreement?
qa.right: To make the team's collaboration rules explicit and revisable
wrong: To bind the team legally
To rate individual performance
To fix individual workloads
qa.why: It captures team-owned rules such as review expectations.

qa.q: What does a platform team treat as its customers?
qa.right: The internal teams that use its services
wrong: The company's executives
External auditors
The finance department
qa.why: Platform teams treat the platform as a product for internal users.
